Oral evidence - 17 Nov 2026

Science and Technology Committee

Oral evidence: Scientific research funding, HC 56

Tuesday 17 November 2026

Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 17 November 2026.

Watch the meeting

Members present: Dame Chi Onwurah (Chair); Emily Darlington; Freddie van Mierlo; Daniel Zeichner.

Questions 98 - 152

Witnesses

I: Professor Jon Butterworth, Professor of Physics, University College London; Professor Catherine Heymans, Astronomer Royal for Scotland and Professor of Astrophysics, University of Edinburgh; Dr Simon Williams, Visiting scientist, Institute for Particle Physics Phenomenology, University of Durham, and Postdoctoral Research Associate, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology; Professor George Efstathiou, Professor of Astrophysics, University of Cambridge.

Examination of witnesses

Witnesses: Professor Jon Butterworth, Professor Catherine Heymans, Dr Simon Williams and Professor George Efstathiou.

Chair: Welcome to today’s meeting of the Science and Technology Committee. It is on a subject that has aroused a great deal of interest and concern: the funding for the Science and Technology Facilities Council. Back in March, we held a session exploring the scientific research funding following reports that there would be reductions in spending. Today, we are going to examine what has changed for researchers, facilities, and international partnerships since March. We are going to look at what the impact has been, whether the prioritisation decisions that were made in July and October and the transitional support have really addressed the issues we identified in March, whether commitments to protect postdoctoral researchers have been delivered, what remains unresolved, and what the impact on the UK’s science base will be in the short, medium, and long-term. It is a science base of which we are obviously so proud.

I am delighted to welcome back three of the witnesses from the March session and a new witness for us today, Professor Efstathiou. Before we start the questions, I should say that the Committee invited representatives of the UK’s three multidisciplinary facilities to join us this morning to give their perspective, but they were unable to attend today. We expect to hear from them in a subsequent session as part of our ongoing scrutiny of this area.

I am going to start on the left and move to the right, which is not something I generally do. I am going to ask each of you to briefly introduce yourselves and give an assessment of the main developments since the Committee last took evidence on this topic in March. Could I start with you, Professor Butterworth?

Professor Butterworth: I am a professor of physics at University College London. I work at CERN on the ATLAS experiment for my research. I should also say that since we were last here, I have been elected president of the Institute of Physics. I am president-elect of the IOP but I am not speaking for the IOP here, I am speaking as an individual professor at the moment. I obviously am in touch with the IOP but I am not speaking with its voice in this meeting.

Since we met, the prioritisation process was gone through, which the community was highly engaged with and the results of which we were told would be published so we could see what had happened. STFC on the back of that actually has not published its prioritisation; it has published the outcomes but it has not published the report. It has published a delivery plan, a statement of how it intends to plan its budgets up to 2029-30. That process was gone through, the outcomes are there, but the rationale and the prioritisation of the experiments are not public.

I said in the last meeting that one of the issues that was very high on the agenda last time was that more or less overnight, the UK had gone 180 degrees on some big infrastructure projects at the end of 2025. Two were in the particle and nuclear area; one was the electron-ion collider that is based in the US, another was an upgrade for the LHCb experiment at CERN. I said about the CERN one in particular that if we did not sort this out, then our name would be mud internationally. Unfortunately, we did not, and it is. That did huge damage to our reputation at CERN.

I have a quote from Professor Marie-Hélène Schune, who is a member of the CNRS Council, a French partner funding body to STFC. She says that it is, “The first time a major European partner has withdrawn from a project that we signed up on—the UK has signed up to it—as highest priority in the European strategy for particle physics.” There are multiple other impacts. It is very damaging to our reputation there. It is damaging to the experiment as well; it will not be able to deliver all its science goals. It is working out now how to de-scope it and try to make it work without the UK contribution.

Another thing worth mentioning, just from the reputational point of view, is that the EIC and LHCb investments were highlighted in the statement from Mark Thomson to be elected as director general of CERN, which the Government also signed up to. That is still having repercussions. These are very close partners we have been working with for years. This looks unprecedented and it has not been addressed at all in the prioritisation process.

Other things that have gone on are the damage to things such as the Quantum Technologies for Fundamental Physics and various other projects that were cancelled in the prioritisation process. That was confirmed. We know that has happened. There was a correction and there was some additional money found—they call it transitional money—which mitigated some cuts in postdocs.

If you remember, there was a statement from the then-Minister, Lord Vallance, that postdoc numbers and the PPAN should be protected. It is clear PPAN has not been protected. On the postdoc numbers, there was some restoration of some cuts but to an already cut number, so it depends on where you start the borderline. We are still at historically low numbers of postdocs in this area now. It is going to decline further over the next few years, according to the delivery plan. I have probably said enough and should let the others go on, but that is what I have seen happen since.

Chair: We will come back to dig deeper into the areas that you described.

Dr Williams: Thank you very much for having me. I am now a postdoctoral researcher at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology in Germany, but I remain a visiting scientist at the Institute for Particle Physics Phenomenology. Since our meeting in March, where we discussed at length the delay to the theory postdoc funding, that funding has come out now and, as Jon said, there has been a small uplift to the number of postdocs in PPAN. We can talk in more detail about how that is uplifted and compared with a different baseline from the number of postdocs who were actually in position last year.

Since then, the biggest thing we have been looking at is how this is affecting early-career researchers. We can talk in more detail but we did a survey, which I updated the Committee on. It shows that 70% of early-career researchers we surveyed currently in position plan to leave the UK for their next position. Some 89% are seriously considering alternatives to a UK PPAN career, and only one in 20 believes they can secure their next position in the UK.

That is telling of the fact that early-career researchers do not feel they are being protected. What we are seeing on the ground suggests that they are not being protected. Anecdotally, everyone I started at the IPPP with in Durham whose contracts ended in 2026 has now moved abroad to countries such as Poland, Germany, the US and Taiwan. We are essentially seeing what I would call a brain drain from the UK because these positions just are not available in the UK.

Chair: When did you move?

Dr Williams: I moved six weeks ago now. I moved in October. I am just back visiting.

Chair: Was your move influenced by this?

Dr Williams: Yes. There were no positions on offer in the UK. I would have liked to remain in the UK. I am very lucky to go to Germany and have the opportunity to go to Germany, but ideally, I would have liked to remain in the UK. Moving countries is very expensive and a big thing to do in your life.

Chair: Also leaving the north-east of England, which we all know is the best area.

Dr Williams: Exactly, yes. It was very hard to leave Durham, that is for sure.

Chair: Yes, okay. I am very sad to hear that.

Professor Heymans: I am a professor at the University of Edinburgh. I am also the Astronomer Royal for Scotland. Last time Jon, Simon, and I were here, we were asking for your help with halting the drastic cuts that were proposed for particle physics, astronomy, and nuclear physics at the time. On behalf of the whole community, I just wanted to extend our thanks to your Committee for genuinely listening to our concerns and for all the work you have been doing to scrutinise the decision-making processes that have been happening at UKRI.

Your question was about what has happened since we were last here. I have been working very closely with the Royal Astronomical Society, and we have been putting in a large number of freedom of information requests to answer some questions we had the last time we were here: how did this happen; how did we get to this point where these drastic cuts were made? I have sent you written evidence with all the information we found through those freedom of information requests and the differences we hear between some ministerial statements and what we are actually experiencing on the ground, which we find very concerning.

One of the other things we have been looking into is exactly how the cuts, which have now been implemented—unfortunately, we did not manage to halt them—are actually impacting our astronomy projects. I remind you that I was in front of your Committee under three years ago now, when your Committee was highlighting the UK as a powerhouse in astronomy and space science. Yet today, 35% of the funding has been cut for our astronomy projects. You might be thinking, how can that be? The headline number from STFC is that PPAN has only been cut by 2.7%. That is a number we just cannot reconcile with what has actually happened.

Over the summer, all the principal investigators across the astronomy projects sent me their planned budgets, which was a flat cash profile across the spending review, and what has happened after these cuts have been implemented. We are losing things such as our ability to develop cutting-edge technology for the Extremely Large Telescope. We are losing our ability to use the entire Earth as a radio telescope to go and take images of supermassive black holes in distant galaxies. The breadth of cuts is very significant. Our wonderful Jodrell Bank Observatory, the e-MERLIN facility there, is due to be closed in 2028.

It is confusing to us to see the cuts that have been implemented and then link those with the numbers we are actually being told by the Ministers. Those particular freedom of information requests that we have put in to try to understand that have been sent back for various reasons. Just to get the budgets I sent you in written evidence took five months of back and forth. That budgetary information would have been available before UKRI was implemented, before that new umbrella institution came in. That is a level of concern.

Last time we were here asking for your help in trying to halt the cuts. Today, I would like to ask for your help in protecting fundamental science as we go forward because UKRI has suggested that this is a short, sharp shock to the system just to get STFC on a sustainable budget. However, none of us have any confidence that it will be sustainable at the end of this spending review because if you are delivering these amazing facilities—for the whole of UK science, it is not just PPAN—you cannot do that on the flat cash envelope it has been given.

Chair: Professor Heymans, exactly what we want to understand here today is what has happened and what the priorities and the process are. We are very proud to be a country that is increasing its investment in science and technology, but within a rising budget it seems astounding that you are facing the kinds of cuts that are certainly in evidence to the Committee.

Freddie van Mierlo: Professor Heymans, since you mentioned Jodrell Bank, something I have followed in the Chamber and Ministers have implied is that the changes have been led by scientific decisions. What is your view on that?

Professor Heymans: Yes, I am sure everyone here has full confidence in the science board that has led that prioritisation exercise because they are our colleagues. They had an impossible task of working out what to cut in a portfolio of 48 different projects, all of which were internationally leading. They had to make very, very difficult decisions. The problem is in how those decisions were made. I will quote you from the STFC minutes, although I hesitate to quote from STFC minutes because the last time I did that in front of you they were changed, or in your own words, actually “Doctored” afterwards. These are minutes from 9 June, that the science board recommendations were, “Based on scientific excellence and impact only and there would be regional impact.”

The Science Council has made it very clear that the prioritisation action was just on science, but we know that our portfolio is so much more than just the science it delivers. Jodrell Bank is a classic example of this. Andy Burnham, our Prime Minister, has talked about his own time as a child visiting the centre. I talked to my colleagues at Jodrell Bank, and nearly half of the visitors say that their prime reason for visiting is because it is a working professional observatory. When you go there and start your visit, the great dish is looking over that way at some black hole, and then by the end of your visit it is turned over there to look at galaxies in the very, very early universe. That type of impact is so much more than just the science that it has delivered.

The other aspect is that Jodrell has just started its amazing programme of space situational awareness. It is amazing what it can do. It can map tumbling space junk that is moving out in space. This is an amazing UK sovereign capability. It is not something that the science board could consider in its prioritisation because it was only looking at the scientific impact, which is in contrast to what the Ministers are saying when they are being asked about the impact assessment. They are saying it was a much broader impact assessment with impacts on these wider questions, and my understanding is that that is not what they have done.

Chair: Right, that is a very important point.

Professor Heymans: It was an impossible task for our science board to deliver. We have to accept its decisions, but the way it is being proposed is that a much broader impact assessment has been done, which simply could not have been done in that timeframe.

Chair: Right, thank you. That is a very important point in terms of the limitations of the Science Council’s criteria, if you like. Professor Efstathiou?

Professor Efstathiou: You can call me George if it is easier. I am an emeritus professor at the University of Cambridge. I was on the science board for five years. My term ended in December 2025. I have previously been on the Council of PPARC, the precursor to STFC, and before that on the APS board at SRC in the long, distant past. I have quite a lot of experience of research council business. I am a cosmologist in discipline.

The main change since your meeting has been the prioritisation exercise and the implementation plan for achieving a balanced budget. I have worked through the numbers and I have real, great concerns about this. With the implementation plan, the PPAN budget is held roughly flat. It is not helpful to our community to be told that the cut is only 2.7% at the end of the spending review period when it is not inflation protected because flat cash is a cut. It is also relevant that the year before the spending review was announced, we had an interim spending review settlement that was flat cash. This means that STFC will have had flat cash allocation for five years.

My colleagues can talk at length about the impact because we have plenty of evidence of the changes that have happened since the spending review and the impact that it has had on PPAN science. I have worked through the numbers and the implementation plan. If there is a commitment to give flat cash to PPAN and then you have the international subscriptions, which are rising slightly lower than the rate of inflation over that period, then the amount of money you have left that is uncommitted that you can work with is relatively small. You take out PPAN and the subscriptions, and that leaves a much smaller amount of money. The cuts then have to be made on that small budget. The impact is that the facilities then get the hit.

Chair: As I understand it, the facilities are facing higher levels of inflation.

Professor Efstathiou: Yes. As the Committee knows, one of the reasons that STFC is more highly exposed to inflationary pressures and shocks to the economy is that the facilities employ a large number of people. It is very difficult to cut the staff level suddenly. In fact, you have to put money in. When I wrote to you after the March session, what concerned me was that it was obvious that if you set the budget at the level that UKRI set the STFC budget, you were going to cause a problem. You did not really have to dig very hard into the numbers to know that this was going to be a very big issue. I could not understand why that had been done because it was creating a problem. We need to explore how that decision was made.

Chair: Sorry, which decision?

Professor Efstathiou: The decision to allocate a flat cash core budget to STFC when it should have been obvious that that was going to cause problems to the facilities and then contagion to PPAN. We need to have a better understanding of how that was made. The UKRI responded by giving transitional funds to PPAN, which is basically an admission that there was a problem with that initial allocation. The transitional funds helped to deal with the difficulty of front-loading cuts; that is what the transitional funds have been used for. If you then look at the way the transitional funds are used in the implementation plan, it tapers off.

However, because the budget is flat cash, the trajectory towards getting a balanced budget looks very unusual. It is basically a ballistic trajectory where you actually hit the target at a steep angle. There is no headroom in this plan to deal with any further shocks to the economy. At the time the allocations were made, there was no war in Iran. We do not know what the future holds. It is very difficult to actually make something that is so sensitive to changes that will actually hit the budget. I do not know what a balanced budget means on a flat cash programme. What budgetary assumptions do you make for future years?

Chair: Thank you, George. If it is okay, I will call you all by your first names now. You have raised a number of issues that we will come back to. As I said, we are trying to understand what the process was. You asked about why the decision was made to allocate a flat cash budget. Who made that decision? We all understand that the Government have to make difficult decisions with regard to taxpayer money and investment. The science budget is rising. If this is a question of allocation within that budget, that is the ministerial responsibility, but I am not clear on the ownership and transparency of that decision.

When Michele Dougherty appeared before us, we talked about inflation and the other financial pressures. She talked about how one of the reasons was the STFC taking on more projects than it could afford. I just want to briefly ask if you think that is a reasonable assessment before we go into the details of scientific prioritisation. You are nodding, Jon.

Professor Butterworth: Yes, I would like to come back on that. I was on the STFC until the beginning of 2025. The element of truth there is that under the previous administration, the STFC was being used as an effective delivery mechanism for a whole bunch of Government priorities. I do not know if you have toured the Harwell site, but it has a lot of activity. It has a very new satellite testing facility, which is Europe leading—maybe world leading—clearly aimed at the space industry and growth. It was given to STFC to deliver, along with the budget. Similarly, there is a National Quantum Computing Centre there. There are a whole bunch of other things that have been going on that were allocated with budgets for the STFC to do.

If you look at the growth in the national labs expenditure, it is going up. That is in the plan, the profile, and that is why it has to be ballistic, as George said. It has to come down very quickly and that will cause huge losses. There was also a pay settlement that was unfunded. All these things, such as the satellite test centre, the National Quantum Computing Centre and other centres that were placed there, were signed off by UKRI, many of them at the ministerial level. The STFC was supposed to deliver them within its budget. It was not that the council was going crazy; the council and the board itself were seen as an effective way of delivering Government priorities and were given the budget to deal with that. That changed when we received the interim settlement of flat cash. Those funding lines were not respected.

By the way, we also were told that the international subscriptions were driving this. They absolutely are not; they are dropping in real terms. There are also ministerial-level, Government-level decisions that UKRI has no control over in the end. It cannot set the budget for CERN. As George was saying, the fact that within that flat cash budget you have this rising inflexibility on the internationals and these huge commitments to centres and Government priorities that were set up under the previous administration, that puts you in an incredibly difficult position when you are hit by a flat cash budget. It is a privilege of a new Government to do that, but you have to accept the consequences. You heard the consequences last time on the bits of the budget that are flexible, which are essentially postdocs and projects.

Chair: We have talked about that. Not to put words in your mouth, but your view then is that the STFC was responding to Government ambitions, which were generally funded, rather than taking on more than it could afford, which was Michele Dougherty’s view. Yes? Does anybody want to add anything to that?

Professor Efstathiou: I was on the science board at those times. The budget for UKRI was rising and the budget for STFC rose. A chief executive of STFC cannot go on a spending spree without the approval of UKRI. It took on additional new facilities. There was investment in the Hartree Centre, the Quantum Computer Service, the Daresbury supercomputer, the National Satellite Test Facility, and importantly, the Diamond-II upgrade, which is a £550 million project.

Chair: Are you saying that the STFC is being made the fall guy for decisions taken by UKRI and the Government?

Professor Efstathiou: Absolutely. I want to say this from a personal point of view because Mark Thomson is the most skilful chief executive I have ever worked with. STFC was on budget in each year of Mark’s term. There is no question of the budget going out of control during that period.

Chair: Before I go to Daniel to look more into the prioritisation exercise we heard about, I just want to clarify with Catherine. I found it very interesting that you spoke about the scientific prioritisation and the board making decisions based on scientific value, rather than also considering social impact. Is it not STFC’s duty to consider the full impact of its spending decisions? Just to be clear, when you talk about the board, it is the STFC board?

Professor Heymans: The PPAN science board has run the prioritisation exercise for the PPAN project. There has been a separate prioritisation exercise done on the facilities and labs side as well, which we know less about as that is not our side of the house. Obviously, the science board’s role is to make that scientific decision. Absolutely. It did it under incredible pressure on an incredibly short timescale. My question is about the way the impact assessment is being portrayed. There have been lots of written parliamentary questions from MPs with concerned constituents saying, “What impact assessment studies have been run?” The stock text that has been responded with in those parliamentary questions suggests that it is a lot more than just a scientific analysis.

What is the impact on universities? There are lots of different dimensions. It is an incredibly complex problem. What is the impact on industry? Let’s take next-generation instrumentation for the Extremely Large Telescope. It is 30 metres across—this thing is huge. It is a major investment from the UK. We have already spent £20 million on two different instruments, which we have now confirmed to the European Southern Observatory community that we have had to pull out of because we are no longer funding that. That money was not going for us to have lovely thoughts about searching for exoplanets that might harbour life; that money was going directly to high-tech engineering and really developing that tech sector.

This prioritisation exercise has cut us back to the point where there is zero ambition whatsoever. There is no room for development or to take new opportunities that are out there. We are getting to the point where in the UK we are going to be experienced in old tech. We are not going to be pushing the technology anymore. That new technology is what we do. That is what we deliver. Again, that has not been factored in. There are a lot of questions. If you are doing it purely on science, which is all that it has done, then obviously we trust what our science board members have come up with.

Chair: We have spent quite a bit of time on the overview of what has happened. That is very useful to understand part of why we are in the position we are in now.

Daniel Zeichner: Good morning, everybody. I would just like to start by going back to Professor Butterworth’s point about how the STFC is almost being used as a fall guy here. We are in an extraordinarily exciting time for science. Huge new opportunities are opening up, which this Committee hears all the time. I slightly got the sense from your comments before that Government were using STFC to try to respond to this change. Have I understood you correctly on that?

Professor Butterworth: You are right that it is a very exciting time; that is for sure. It is true. The UK has a world-leading position in this, which is obviously under threat in many, many ways with this. Under the previous executive you saw the ecosystem of research and innovation being developed extremely effectively. You were leveraging our excellence in asking the big PPAN questions, “What is the universe made of? How did we get here?” You were leveraging that to at the same time, on the same site, with the same partners and universities, deliver satellite testing facilities that mostly will launch commercial satellites, not science ones. That is true of the Hartree Centre at Daresbury, which is also similar. It is a major computing centre that was one of the things STFC was given to deliver. There has been huge industry engagement, also doing a lot of really basic, exciting science.

That ecosystem should be one of our strengths, right? The current leadership of UKRI and the Government see that strength and want to make the most of it. They are strangling part of the ecosystem to strengthen another bit. You need it all. The areas of science we are talking about here, which we basically work in, are what attract people into the field. There is good evidence that this is one of the things. Those people do not stay and do only these things. As Catherine was saying, they start developing world-leading technologies. The things STFC was asked to deliver were actually very well aligned with that. They were really exploiting the synergies between the basic science, cutting-edge technology, industry involvement and training. It was going great, to be honest. It is a real shame we are in this position.

Dr Williams: Maybe I could just add something very briefly. Often when we look at the problem, we say, “Okay, this is the blue-sky physics, this is the curiosity physics, these are the cutting-edge technologies that the Government are interested in.” I work in quantum computing. We are developing algorithms for quantum computers. I work closely with IBM and other companies. This just shows you the synergies between the whole of the ecosystem; it cannot be compartmentalised.

Daniel Zeichner: That brings me to my next question, which is really on the prioritisation exercise from July. Could you all briefly comment on your view on the success or otherwise of that process? You all have experience of being involved in these difficult decisions.

Professor Butterworth: First, it has not released the rationale behind it, which it promised to do. Judging from the impacts, as Catherine said, it was given in quite narrow terms: what is the science impact? Most of us are not going to argue with that although, without seeing the rationale, it seems very strange, for instance, that LHCb was not prioritised for future funding given what we know about the priority nationally and internationally. We have not seen the rationale for that, so we do not know.

It confirmed a whole bunch of things that had already been said. The plasma wakefield acceleration experiment at CERN was cancelled. The Quantum Technologies for Fundamental Physics, which was a great example of these synergies, in my opinion, was cancelled. We already knew that in March and all the prioritisation did was just say, “Yes, that’s still going on.” I have a real problem with the fact that while I have confidence with the people on the science board, I do not know how many of its actual recommendations emerged in the prioritisation that STFC eventually put out because we have not seen the report from the science board to STFC and UKRI.

It is hard to comment further on that, really. I find some things that were not prioritised very striking. It is very puzzling why they were not prioritised. Maybe I have not seen all the evidence, so maybe the science board was right, or maybe that is not what it said. We have not seen the report.

Professor Heymans: George and I had a call with all the principal investigators on the astronomy side the other day. We heard from Keith Grainge, who is the chair of the science board, about why there were delays in his report coming out. It would appear that there has been a lot of back and forth. The PIs on the astronomy side were unanimous that we were very concerned that we were hearing that the chair of UKRI, Ian Chapman, had been making recommendations and requests to re-scope that project report. It is an independent expert advisory panel; it should be able to write its report. For sure, UKRI can redact parts that it considers to be confidential, but for there to be requests to re-scope it? We all found that—well, one person said they were incredulous about it.

We have had lots of projects on the astronomy side that are relatively inexpensive—under £100,000 per year—that have been cut in their entirety. They are obviously now scrabbling around for alternative sources of funding. It is very hard for them to get that without saying why they were cut because obviously if you say to alternative funders, “The science board says, ‘You’re not internationally leading, and therefore we shouldn’t fund you,’” that is not what the science board has said. Everything was internationally leading but until that report comes out, it is very hard for our other projects.

For example, there is one instrument that has currently lost its operational funding for searching for Earth 2.0. How cool is that? It should be able to find alternative funding hopefully because it is not that much money, but it cannot do that without that report to explain why it was not funded. The more you can do to help us get that report out, the better. I should also add, for our friends on the facilities and labs side, at least we are talking about the possibility of a report coming out. On the facilities and labs side there is no report. There has been very little communication on the facilities side about how that prioritisation exercise was run, which is very concerning for our friends on the other side of the STFC house.

Daniel Zeichner: George, you wrote to us back in March and made some very strong points and criticised the governance structure that is creating a bias towards facilities at the expense of the PPAN programme. My understanding is that this is not a new problem. This is a debate that has gone on for quite a long time. What would you suggest is done?

Professor Efstathiou: I was concerned about how the composition of STFC could bias funding in favour of the facilities at the expense of PPAN. In reality, now that we have seen the outcome of the prioritisation exercise, there was no alternative given the budget than to hit the facilities very hard. However, because of the difficulties, there is still the possibility of further contagion and cuts in the PPAN budget.

The one feature of doing this kind of prioritisation exercise is that, in my experience of the programme managers at STFC, they are incredibly helpful. They really try to help the community and extract the most science they can from the funding. The science board can give us an assessment of scientific quality. It is not a linear relation because if you look at the portfolio of projects, there are the big projects such as CMS, ATLAS, SKA and ESA, which you cannot touch really, otherwise the programme does not make any sense. There is then a large number of smaller projects and if you cut them all, you do not cut a lot of the budget. That is the problem. With the prioritisation exercise we have seen a lot of really disappointed people who have had their projects cut. It is not necessarily saving a lot of money.

Freddie van Mierlo: I just had a follow-up question to George, based on what you were saying. The Committee has had evidence from the previous Secretary of State for DSIT and then a Minister of State for DBIST. When we asked the question, basically, “Your job is to set the budget; do you care, frankly, about what the impact of that is and how that is materialised?” The answer from them both, frankly, is, “No. We’re responsible for setting the budget and it’s down to UKRI and STFC to distribute it as best they can or as they see fit.” Do you think it is right that Ministers are so distant from the decisions that are being taken by the council?

Professor Efstathiou: To get to the nub of what has happened and why STFC and the other research councils are experiencing difficulty because of this flat cash issue, there has been a policy shift. We do not really understand the policy shift. Just looking at the numbers, what happened is that the core budgets to the research councils were left at flat cash. In the case of STFC, I would argue that it was actually cut below the level and then set at flat cash. Bear in mind we have had an increase. The increase goes from £9.2 billion to £9.986 billion.

The money that was released went in to promoting buckets two and three. That is a policy decision. It is taking money out of basic research. We are not aware that any impact assessment was ever made of what the consequences of this would be. There was no discussion with the community on making such a big change to the science budget. That is actually the reason you have so many scientists now complaining when we had a budget increase. We do not want to be here doing this sort of thing. We would rather be doing science and delivering science on the extra money that was allocated in a time when we do understand the pressures.

Chair: Can you just clarify something? You say that you understand money has been moved between buckets. How much money has been moved between the buckets?

Professor Efstathiou: I have the summary here.

Diamond is basically a particle accelerator, like CERN. I should clarify that I am certainly not a user of the national labs and these facilities but I talked to some users. Somebody said to me that the majority of users are not aware of what is about to happen. We have been complaining about the comms and the lack of transparency on the PPAN side. It is even worse on the facilities side. The fact that there is not even a discussion about a report coming out from their science board is alarming.

I have spoken to people on their science board. They said that the depths of the cuts they had to implement on the facilities side extended well into the line items that they had considered at really high risk of a loss of the UK sovereign capability. However, you have to ask those questions to our colleagues on the facilities because it is not really something that we can comment on.

It is important to remember here that these national facilities deliver for all sectors of UK science. There was a very interesting article from a dementia researcher saying that his colleagues had absolutely no idea that their research on dementia was going to be impacted by the facilities. I had no idea that our facilities were helping dementia research, antimicrobial research—there are so many different areas that the facilities deliver: AI, green energy, biotech, agrotech. It is everything. If you are cutting the facilities to such an extent as they are talking about—we talked about efficiency savings earlier—it is very hard to make those efficiency savings. This will be shutting down facilities unless they can make the revenue that we were talking about earlier.

Professor Efstathiou: That does not help very much.

Professor Heymans: That is not going to help. Unfortunately, we are not really the right people to ask those questions. I worry on the timeframe just because that voluntary exit scheme is already in play with no clear strategy in place, at least to my colleagues on the facilities side.

Freddie van Mierlo: You are absolutely right to point out that it is a real shame that your colleagues on the facilities side have not been able to come forward. As far as I can see, they have been gagged by UKRI and the Labour Government, frankly. I find it astonishing that a Labour Government would be gagging or overseeing that, when they should be on the side of workers, who should be able to come forward and speak to us plainly. I hope they do, or that they are given permission to do so in the new year. Maybe if I speak to George because it is your—

Chair: Just to clarify, they certainly do not say that they have been gagged but they are saying that they could not come. I just wanted to clarify that but obviously you can have your opinion.

Freddie van Mierlo: That would be my opinion then, for the record. Yes, I would like to ask George because it is your responsibility as a panel to stick up for the facilities side, which you have been doing. What would your view be on what capabilities have so far already been lost and withdrawn?

Professor Efstathiou: I do not know the exact answer to your question about what has happened since the spending review. However, the facilities side is the most multidisciplinary part of the STFC portfolio. It serves universities, basic research and industry. In the implementation plan there will be a gateway point in 2027 and then a second gateway point in 2028. Should they fail to meet their cuts by one or both of those gateways, then the default position is to close the facility. There is a lot of concern that the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source will be the most vulnerable facility to be closed. It is amazing that we had an expansion of the facilities with Government approval and now we are imposing hard cuts. That wastes money.

Freddie van Mierlo: You are referring to the half a billion pounds that was invested into Diamond?

Professor Efstathiou: No, as far as I know the £550 million investment in Diamond-II is still going ahead. Really, if we lose that capability then it is the premier facility at the Harwell site, but my understanding is that will continue.

Freddie van Mierlo: One thing I am trying to get to is that the Government keep insisting that the three facilities will remain operational, but again, operational is probably a word that is doing a lot of heavy lifting. What do you think that means?

Professor Efstathiou: In the time of the Ukraine crisis, which put pressure on STFC, STFC decided to cut time. It decided to not keep them operational 100% of the time.

Freddie van Mierlo: Again, the Government could claim that they are keeping the three sites operational when in fact they are being run at a reduced capacity.

Professor Efstathiou: Yes.

Freddie van Mierlo: They could still make that claim. That is similar to other ways they are claiming that there are no cuts, it is flat etc. It leads to this level of frustration that we are seeing where the Government are not really owning up to what is happening.

Professor Heymans: I am unclear whether it is the Government or UKRI. One of the interesting things we have been trying to understand in the written evidence we have submitted to you is that the statements being made by Chris McDonald do not always connect with official minutes from STFC, or with how we are seeing things on the board. It is genuinely unclear to me where that decision making is happening. A classic example is that Chris McDonald said there had been no international reviewers of the science prioritisation report, whereas we know international colleagues who submitted feedback on it. That is just a really strange example of where something has happened.

It is unclear to me whether this is Government or UKRI. I do not know where these decisions are being made. We had this discussion when we were here back in March. Who made this decision? We still do not know the answer to that. You said that if it was Government Ministers, they should own it. If it is UKRI, then it should be clear with Government Ministers how that decision has been taken and why. At the moment it is unclear to us.

Freddie van Mierlo: That sounds absolutely right to me. If I could ask George one more follow-up on this, how confident are you that the three facilities—the Central Laser Facility, ISIS and Diamond—will remain operational?

Professor Efstathiou: I am not optimistic. My guess is that the first gateway in 2027 will fail.

Freddie van Mierlo: The Government have been very clear, to their credit at least, that at that point that would mean potentially closing one of them.

Professor Efstathiou: Yes. We ought to be concerned about the wastage of money—of money that has been invested.

Professor Butterworth: I will make an interjection there. Again, as the others, I am not a facilities expert. On the neutron sources in particular, there is a European spallation source under construction in Sweden, which we are a partner in. There is a real opportunity here—in the spirit of rapprochement with Europe as well maybe—to make maybe more of an international, European-wide coherent plan about how ISIS, the ESS and ILL, which is the other source in France that we are also a partner in, all work together. That maybe means internationalising facilities in the UK and asking our international partners to foot some of the bill, which of course is not great when we have just been annoying them all enormously by not paying our way on other things.

Nevertheless, there may be opportunities there. However, I am speaking way above my pay grade here. Just having been on STFC, this is something that was always an elephant in the room that was never fully addressed.

Freddie van Mierlo: It is a classic by-product, if you like, of discussions about closures and cuts, that people start leaving as well. It is always the case that the best people leave first when there is uncertainty. What is your estimation of morale at these facilities? What are we going to be left with if we do not get clarity soon?

Professor Efstathiou: I can only answer that on hearsay, but morale is very low. On the PPAN side there is also a lot of frustration.

Professor Butterworth: The labs are more than the facilities as well. There are the technology centres, there is RAL Space, there are all these other things. Overall, there is a pile of gloom.

Freddie van Mierlo: Sorry, I have one more question if that is all right. This is slightly broader and more general. When you look at the size of the cuts that are needed, they are big in terms of STFC but probably reasonably small when you look at global Government spending. How frustrated are you about that?

When you perhaps look at the budget, one thing that really struck me—this is maybe a bit more political—is the giveaway of £100 for every household between bands A and D. On the face of it, everyone is facing a cost of living crisis and people need a bit of relief from that. It also seems quite untargeted. As I live in a band D property, I will be eligible for it. I will be honest; I do not really need it. It will not make much difference. It is costing £2.8 billion. When you look at that, do you feel a bit aggrieved that there is £2.8 billion being spent, when you would only require a fraction of that?

Professor Efstathiou: No. The reason for that is that we all have an awareness of the pressures right now. Just today, more money is needed to deal with the NEET problem. The police are saying that they cannot cope with the budgets they have. We are aware of the pressures. I am concerned that a budget for science has been allocated, it goes from £9.2 billion to £10 billion, and it has been misused. I would rather that that budget was used effectively, instead of creating the crisis we have.

Chair: That is very clear. I just want to pick up a couple of points about international reputation, which in practice you have answered, and then we will finish by 11.30 am. We have talked about how international science is and specifically the cuts to the UK physics community but also to international programmes. What are you actually hearing from the physics community in this country and international partners abroad about the impact on our reputation and our attractiveness for collaboration?

Professor Butterworth: I think I am talking for PPAN in general, so astro and particle: the UK has never had a reputation for being lavish. It has never had enough money to do everything it wanted to do but it has always delivered. Whatever we have promised, we have delivered. We have had the people to do it, we have had a sensible reprofiling when projects hit trouble, we have been good people to have on your side when a project runs into trouble. For my whole career, that has been our reputation in all our work we did. I worked in Hamburg at DESY and at CERN. It has also been true in Fermilab in the US and, from what I have seen, at the Council and UCL on various astrophysical projects.

That is a really precious reputation and that has been absolutely shot in the foot by the LHCb decision because the signals that were going out on Government-approved documents were that we were keen on this and we were going to be good partners. Then overnight that just changed. People have not seen that before. The shock is still being felt. That has damaged us hugely. It may be recoverable, but it is really sad to see. To me that is the most important thing. Simon can speak to things such as the postdoc recruitment, which has also had an impact, but for me it is this project partnership part. We have always paid our CERN subscription on time. We have always done what we said we would do on a project. That has been hit very badly.

Dr Williams: The speed and almost the carelessness of these cuts have had such an impact, which was not assessed before, to my knowledge at least. In our survey, 75% of those whose contracts end this year have not secured the next position. That is 75% of the surveyed people who are very highly trained and do not have a position to go to. Where do they turn to next? They turn to countries that have these stable and more reassuring funding streams.

Of my friends who have moved abroad, everyone always saw the UK as being a brilliant place to come and get research experience, but those opportunities just are not there. In the postdoc world you take the opportunities that are there, and so they have gone abroad. The speed and how these decisions have been made will have an impact for a long time that is going to be hard to repair.

Chair: That is sobering.

Professor Heymans: On the international side, people are just shocked and surprised. This is not what the UK does. The equivalent of the LHCb on the astronomy side is the very long-term, decade-long preparation we have had for the Extremely Large Telescope. There has been £20 million of investment so far in two instruments that we have just had to say to our colleagues that we have had to pull out of.

It is not just the large scales as well. We have lots of wonderful small-scale experiments that deliver amazing things. There is an instrument in La Palma that recently featured on the television as a really exciting new experiment. It allows us to find exoplanets and things that are changing in our night sky. It costs absolute peanuts. We are talking £60,000 a year. That has now been completely cut. It looks like it will be given to the Spanish and the GranTeCan telescope. This is huge amounts of UK investment. Actually, it is a small amount. Our international colleagues are just a bit baffled, they are saying, “Well why did you invest so much just to pull out?”

Chair: Yes, that is very concerning. Just as a point of comparison, how can I put this? The United States has not been a consistent scientific investor over the last two years or more, shall we say? Is international physics talent attracted to the European Union? Are we disadvantaged even in comparison with the US or are there other emerging countries in physics excellence, particularly?

Dr Williams: From the experience of people I know, it seems to be worldwide. Lots of my colleagues I worked in Durham with have gone to Europe, mainly because they are European so it is not so far to go. Others have gone to Taiwan. I know some people who have taken up or are looking at taking up positions in China. We also have some who have gone to the US. Obviously, yes, the US has been volatile in the last few years. There is an influx of people from there as well. One could argue that it is also going through a brain drain but at a potentially different level just because of the size of its research base.

Professor Butterworth: Just in terms of project delivery, which is the other part when you join a construction project, the US is so much bigger than the UK and I would describe it as having been lavish in other cases. It makes up for that volatility in terms of the sheer amount of resource it has. Where it has really had the biggest impact in project delivery has been with our European partners, who are our peers. We rely on each other, and then it is as though one of the pillars has gone.

Chair: Okay, that is a very important point. One of the things this Committee is really interested in understanding is that curiosity-driven research is said to have been protected, as we have talked about, and yet we hear so many examples of negative impact on that. We will be talking to the multidisciplinary facilities in the near future. I visited Boulby Mine physics lab—

Professor Heymans: Did you wear a hat, Dame Chi?

Chair: I had to wear two different hats. One for the mine and one for the physics. It is a working mine. It is the deepest mine in the UK. There is absolutely amazing physics being done there, trying to identify dark matter. I was also struck by how there were vertical farms. There was a wide range of amazing science going on. Is it possible to protect curiosity-driven research while undermining multidisciplinary facilities? It is a yes or no question there. I seem to have silenced you.

Professor Butterworth: I thought you were asking Catherine.

Professor Heymans: I would say no, you cannot.

Professor Butterworth: That is right. The facilities provide the capability to do the curiosity-led research. You can be as curious as you like–

Chair: But if you have no facilities!

Professor Butterworth: Even the theorists will run out of things to be curious about if you are not pushing the technologies and you do not have the facilities to address the questions they are interested in. Simon does not want to write programmes for computers that never get built. Boulby is one of the places where they might be hosted.

Chair: I certainly hope so as it is in North Yorkshire and not so far from me, as well as the fantastic science that is going on and having it in a mine. Finally, my colleague Freddie challenged the Government on ensuring that academic voices or voices in our research community could feel that they could speak honestly and clearly, which is important to our process of scrutinising and to confidence and trust in the sector. You have spoken out passionately, clearly and critically. I hope you feel that you have that freedom to do so.

I would also just say on the Committee’s behalf that if there is anyone watching or listening to this who does not feel they have that freedom to do so, they can contact us anonymously, or they can contact us and their evidence will be treated confidentially. It is really important that we hear from all voices, irrespective of how they are being funded.

We have a number of actions we are taking, particularly understanding how the facilities boards have come to their decision, getting the report from the science board, and clarifying in terms of some funding streams. As we have agreed, it is going to be difficult to follow funding streams. We will be following up on that, but can I just really say a huge thank you. This is a complex subject, which has real-life implications for researchers, our economic science base and prosperity across our country. You have shared your views, expertise and experience with us in a way that is both engaging and credible. Thank you very much for that.
